json.title: INSPECT: the per-device snapshot event — one `device.inventory` per device per pass, fattened at enqueue

labels.name: v0-blocker
labels.description: V0 contract item that other V0 work depends on

json.body:
> **Anchors in this issue are cited against `da4e444`.** Main is now `6e75c6d`; #240, #246, #247, #252 and #253 merged since. Resolve line numbers against `da4e444`, not against main — the rebase note in the comments says what moved.

*Evidence verified against `main` @ `da4e444` (PR #239, merged 2026-09-02, moved lines in `backend/app/models/schema.py`, `backend/app/catalog/service.py` and `docs/posture-snapshot.md`; the citations into those files are post-#239, every other cited file is unchanged since `82aed70`). Split from #81 (v0 blocker 1), which stays the contract record. This session runs first; #242 runs second and reads the payload this issue defines. #243 is independent of both; `key_bundle` is v1 (#245).*

## Why now

Every ruling the snapshot needed is now on the record, and the thing itself is not built. #81 ruling 1 — one event per installed app, Jamf's object untouched — has stood since 2026-08-24. The vocabulary it travels under was frozen on 2026-09-01 (#188, PR #228, `docs/splunk-wire-vocabulary.md`); the meta block and the envelope it rides shipped in PR #191 (`_device_meta`, `backend/app/mdm/service.py:812-870`; `backend/app/core/wire.py`) and reached every family in PR #204. Kyle answered the two questions that gated the build on 2026-09-02 — Jamf's v4 names verbatim, and fatten at enqueue — and both are recorded on #81's ruling comment (the 2026-09-02 rulings).

What is missing is the event the fan-out expands. `_build_body` cannot expand what it does not receive — it sees the destination and the stored payload and nothing else (`backend/app/core/outbox.py:109-143`) — and today the payload is a delta that exists only when an app moved. So #242 is blocked on this, #222 is blocked on the fan-out, and #81 carries `v0-blocker` until both merge. The flip is ~2026-09-17.

## What ships today

`process_sync` (`backend/app/mdm/service.py:873`) emits one event, `device.inventory.changed`, and only when the app list moved:

```python
    if not added and not removed_rows:
        await db.commit()
        return None
```
`backend/app/mdm/service.py:992-994`

A device whose apps did not change produces nothing. `test_a_sync_enqueues_one_event_per_changed_device_and_nothing_for_the_rest` (`backend/tests/test_outbox_passes_db.py:545-575`) pins the second sweep of an unchanged fleet at zero device events, and its docstring calls that "the number #81 rewrites"; `test_wire_casing.py:161-175` has to move an app on purpose just to get an inventory event to judge. The one event that does exist carries `addedApps`/`removedApps` as `NormalizedApp` lists — `name`, `bundleId`, `version`, `shortVersion` (always null from the Jamf normalizer, `backend/app/mdm/jamf/client.py:737-741`) plus the four minted identity fields (`backend/app/schemas/payload.py:31-53`) — and `deviceMeta` (`payload.py:133`). `KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES` has four members (`outbox.py:21`); a type not in it can be neither produced nor subscribed to (`outbox.py:23`, `backend/app/schemas/destinations.py:55-61`).

No *state* event on the wire today carries `path`, `cfBundleShortVersionString`, `cfBundleVersion` or `macAppStore`, and none carries any section other than applications. (`device.change` does carry them — the canonical entry body as `old`/`new` on an application change, and per-field values for the scalar sections: `backend/app/changes/derive.py:148-158`, `:192-204`, `:311-318` — but that family says what happened, not what is, #81 ruling 6, and it is not the family this issue adds to.)

## What is ruled, and where — not re-litigated here

| Ruling | Record |
| --- | --- |
| One snapshot stream, per app; Jamf's object untouched | #81 ruling 1 |
| Jamf's v4 names, verbatim. Kyle, 2026-09-02: "Use Jamf's v4 Names Verbatim in the sections I am copying them." Kyle, 2026-09-01: "I leave the jamf data as is when copying it over to the record under the `apps` key so leave as is. I don't want to change that or take on that ETL work." He ruled the *names*; the field set is the next row | #81 ruling comment, 2026-09-02 |
| Fatten at enqueue; no delivery-time join. Kyle, 2026-09-02: "flatten at enqueue" — read as *fatten*, the option he confirmed on 2026-09-01 with "both answers aren't great, but I think that is the better one." | #81 ruling comment, 2026-09-02; #81 spike comment Q2 |
| Field set on the app object = the ledger's allowlist: `name`, `path`, `version`, `cfBundleShortVersionString`, `cfBundleVersion`, `bundleId`, `macAppStore`. `sizeMegabytes`, `updateAvailable`, `externalVersionId` stay off. A **labelled assumption**, not his words — the spike's sub-decision A (telemetry rides) was not separately accepted | `backend/app/mdm/jamf/contract.py:322-336`; #81 ruling comment (recorded there as an assumption) |
| Wrapper keys and sourcetypes: the frozen registry, generated from `SECTIONS` | `docs/splunk-wire-vocabulary.md` §2; `backend/app/core/wire_vocabulary.py:46-63` |
| `patch` and `vuln` are inline enrichments on the app sub-event | `wire_vocabulary.py:65-75` |
| `patch.supported`: a bool, always present, `false` when no Jamf Patch title matches. Kyle, 2026-09-01: "we need a default for the patching... Probably a boolean that says `patchingSupport` and set that equal to false. That way you can always search for it or not it easy." | #81 ruling comment, 2026-09-02 |
| `vuln.assessment` ∈ `covered` \| `unknown_app` \| `off`, always present; ships `off` until #113's work lands | #113, ruled 2026-09-01; #81 ruling comment |
| The minted identity fields (`appHash`, `versionHash`, `keyTitle`, `keyFull`) do not ride the sub-events in v0. Kyle, 2026-09-02: "leave them out for now we can add them in the future. We can add keys later but we can't take them away." | #81 ruling comment, 2026-09-02 |
| Aperture: `apps is None` = outside the read, touch nothing; `[]` = read and genuinely empty; read per section on the snapshot | `service.py:881-888`; `payload.py:76-79`; Kyle, 2026-08-29; #81 ruling comment |
| `deviceMeta`: the block as built, nulls dropped, `eventID = uuid5(jobID, jamfProID)` | `service.py:812-870`; `docs/runs.md:107-130`. #189 owns the block, including any drift between its 2026-08-31 table and what is built; nothing here adds or moves a key |
| Envelope: `time` from the event's own timestamp, `host` in both places on purpose, `source` = the instance | `wire.py:68-91`; `outbox.py:121-130` |
| Casing: camelCase, the token `ID` uppercase, a vendor's key keeps the vendor's spelling | `docs/splunk-wire-vocabulary.md` §4 |
| Additive-only clauses 1–6 | `wire_vocabulary.py:118-133` |

## The design

### One event, `device.inventory`

One `device.inventory` per device per ingest that passes the ledger's monotonic guard, whether or not anything changed. It fires from `process_sync`, in the same transaction as the ledger write and the row updates — `ingest_computer` promises exactly that (`service.py:644-645`), and so does `enqueue_event` (`outbox.py:75-77`). It does **not** fire on the stale path (`service.py:657-672` returns before `process_sync` is reached), and not for a device whose ingest raised and was rolled back (`service.py:527-533`).

The name is a recommendation, not a ruling. `device.inventory` is the state; `device.inventory.changed` is what happened to it — #81 ruling 6's IS/HAPPENED test applied to the discriminator — so the delta keeps its name and keeps shipping unchanged, which is what generic webhooks and change derivation were promised in #81's body. `event` stays the one discriminator on every family (`docs/runs.md:142-148`); `event=device.inventory*` then collects the state and its deltas together and `event=device.inventory.changed` is untouched. Alternatives the session may prefer, named so they are rejected rather than missed: `device.inventory.snapshot` (says what it is, but pairs oddly with `.changed` as a sibling suffix on the same noun) and `device.snapshot` (drops the noun the delta family already uses).

### The payload — proposed shape; the session finalises it inside the rulings

```json
{
  "event": "device.inventory",
  "occurredAt": "2026-09-02T02:00:00+00:00",
  "deviceMeta": { "jobID": "…", "trigger": "sweep", "eventID": "…", "…": "the built #189 block, unchanged" },

  "general":         { "…": "Jamf's object, Jamf's keys, the contract's allowlist" },
  "hardware":        { "…": "…" },
  "operatingSystem": { "…": "…" },
  "userAndLocation": { "…": "…" },
  "purchasing":      { "…": "…" },
  "security":        { "…": "…" },
  "diskEncryption":  { "…": "…" },

  "app": [
    { "app":   { "name": "Maps.app", "path": "/System/Applications/Maps.app", "version": "3.0",
                 "cfBundleShortVersionString": "3.0", "cfBundleVersion": "2972.20.6.12.13",
                 "bundleId": "com.apple.Maps", "macAppStore": false },
      "patch": { "supported": false },
      "vuln":  { "assessment": "off" } }
  ],
  "ea":               [ { "ea":               { "definitionId": "…", "name": "…", "values": ["…"] } } ],
  "group":            [ { "group":            { "groupId": "…", "groupName": "…", "smartGroup": true } } ],
  "profile":          [ { "profile":          { "…": "…" } } ],
  "localUserAccount": [ { "localUserAccount": { "…": "…" } } ],
  "cert":             [ { "cert":             { "…": "…" } } ],
  "update":           [ { "update":           { "…": "…" } } ]
}
```

(The Maps.app values are the first `applications[]` entry of `backend/tests/fixtures/jamf/computer_inventory_detail_real.json`, with its three telemetry fields removed.)

Four properties, each traceable to a ruling:

1. **The wrapper keys are the registry's and nothing else.** Fourteen possible section keys, exactly `SECTION_WRAPPERS.values()` (`wire_vocabulary.py:46-63`): the seven scalar sections are objects, the seven list sections are lists. The registry's own comment groups `localUserAccount` under "one per device — long" (`wire_vocabulary.py:47-55`); that is the naming rule, and the contract's `entry_kind` makes it a list (`contract.py:425-428`) — the list wins. The scalar ones are what #81 called the "device anchor" — under the frozen registry the anchor is not one sub-event but one per scalar section (`loon:jamf:mac:general`, `…:hardware`, and so on), which is why all seven ride here.
2. **A list item is the sub-event body, minus `deviceMeta`.** `{"app": {…Jamf…}, "patch": {…}, "vuln": {…}}` is, byte for byte, what #242 emits under `loon:jamf:mac:app` once it adds the block, the envelope and (its decision D1) the `event` key — so the fan-out is iteration, not reshaping, and every shape decision lives on this side of the outbox, where the data is. It also keeps LoonInspect's enrichment keys *beside* Jamf's object rather than inside it: the standing "namespaced, not flattened" answer (`docs/splunk-wire-vocabulary.md:44-47`), and the guarantee that Jamf can never add a field that collides with `patch`. The price is `app[].app.bundleId` on a generic-webhook or Elastic document. The alternative — bare Jamf objects in the list, with the fan-out hoisting enrichment keys back out of them — puts the same decision in two places. Session's call; written down so it is a decision.
3. **Jamf's names; the allowlist's fields.** Every section object is Jamf's v4 object under Jamf's keys, restricted to the contract's allowlist for that section (`contract.py:199-397`). For the app object this is the reading #81's comment records, labelled as an assumption: Kyle ruled the *names*; the field set is the reading of "leave the jamf data as is", and the one point he may want to overrule. For the other thirteen sections it is a second labelled **assumption**: "in the sections I am copying them" read as the same rule everywhere — Jamf's names, not Jamf's every field. Consequence worth saying out loud: the telemetry the allowlist excludes (`lastContactTime`, `lastIpAddress`, `reportDate`, battery — `contract.py:222-225`, `:253-254`; disk free is a section v0 never reads, `contract.py:26-28`) is off the wire in v0. Additive later under clause 1; `lastReportDate` already rides `deviceMeta`.
4. **Labelled entries carry their label under Jamf's key.** The contract keeps names out of the *hash* — "names of Jamf objects are labels, not content" (`contract.py:29-34`) — and carries them beside the body as `Entry.label` (`contract.py:527-531`). The wire wants the name: `ea.name`, `group.groupName`, `profile.displayName` are what an analyst types. So the item is the entry body plus the label under the key Jamf spells it with (`entry_label`, `contract.py:415-423`). This is what #197 asks of the EA object — keyed on `definitionId`, with `name` carried as the label (#197: "the contract keys on `definitionId`", and name "is the label").

Top level: `event`, `occurredAt`, `deviceMeta`, the section wrappers. Recommend *not* copying the delta's `provider` and `deviceExternalID` onto the snapshot — both are already `deviceMeta.jamfProID` and the sourcetype's vendor segment, and a key that ships is never removed (clause 3).

Three meanings of absence, all written into the doc. `{}` or `[]`: read and genuinely empty. A section wrapper absent: the section was outside this read's aperture — a second meaning for a missing key beside clause 4's single one, "Absence of a key means the event predates it, never that its value is 'none'" (`wire_vocabulary.py:125-127`; `docs/splunk-wire-vocabulary.md:142-144`). Clause 4 is frozen and held in step with the doc by `tests/test_wire_vocabulary.py:104-110`, so the doc states the wrapper rule as a per-event exception a consumer can rely on — a missing wrapper means "not observed in this pull", never empty — and the session says which it did: amended the clause text (`ADDITIVE_ONLY_CLAUSES` and the doc together), or left the clause and recorded the wrapper rule beside it as the aperture's, not the vocabulary's. (The spike's carve-out — no snapshot when a section is unread — avoids the collision; see Aperture.) A key absent inside a Jamf object: Jamf sent no value — an older server that does not report the field (`contract.py:326-330`), or a null or empty value the canonicalizer dropped under (a) below. The additive-only clauses govern LoonInspect's own keys; they never describe Jamf's object, whose one wire-level guarantee is the v4 pin under Docs.

### Where the data is already in hand

- `ingest_computer` holds `raw` (`service.py:631`) and the canonical `Observation` it built from it (`observation = canonicalize_computer(...)`, `:647`), then hands `process_sync` only `normalize_computer(raw, sections)` (`:692`). The `Observation` (`contract.py:492-505`) is `sections: dict[str, SectionContent]` — scalar sections as a canonical body (`:476-479`), list sections as deduplicated, digest-ordered `Entry` tuples each carrying `body` and `label` (`:468-472`, `:516-532`) — with nested EAs already merged and the quarantine already applied (`:543-563`). It is, section for section, the allowlisted view of the record the ledger just wrote.
- `process_sync` eagerly loads `existing.apps` (`:899-900`), and after `record_device_apps` at `:990` those `InstalledApp` rows carry the Jamf Patch answer — `jamf_title_ids`, `patch_state`, `this_version_seen`, `latest_version`, `latest_released_at`, and since PR #239 `releases_missed` (`backend/app/models/schema.py:212-226`), copied onto the row by `copy_answer` (`backend/app/catalog/service.py:138-150`). `patch.supported` is a read of a row already in the transaction — "no join anywhere", as the spike put it. Cache, don't calculate (`docs/app-catalog.md:11-15`).
- `_device_meta(existing)` and `envelope(...)` are built at `:1021` and `:1032-1036` for the delta; the snapshot calls the same two functions with the same arguments.

So the seam change is small and specific: `process_sync` must receive the observation (a keyword parameter; one call site, `:692`, and no test calls `process_sync` directly) and enqueue the snapshot **before** the early return at `:992-994`, inside the transaction that `:993` and `:1038` commit.

One hazard, stated so the test catches it: after `db.delete(row)` at `:966` and the flush at `:983`, the in-memory `existing.apps` collection can still hold the removed rows — SQLAlchemy does not prune a loaded collection on delete. `record_device_apps` already re-selects by `device_id` rather than reading `existing.apps` (`catalog/service.py:158`); the snapshot's patch join should read rows the same way, or build the current set as `previous_hashes` minus `removed_rows` plus `added`. A removed app must not appear in the snapshot; assert it.

### The four fields the installed-apps table does not hold — the decision, with a recommendation and the trade

`installed_apps` holds `name`, `bundle_id`, `version`, `short_version`, the hashes and the patch columns (`schema.py:187-226`) — no `path`, `cfBundleShortVersionString`, `cfBundleVersion`, `macAppStore`. Two sources were on the table:

**(a) Read the canonical observation.** The entry bodies at `observation.sections["applications"].entries[*].body` hold at most the seven allowlisted fields, each absent where Jamf sent null or omitted it. Free: no schema change, no second write path, the object already in hand, and a payload that is self-contained — it never couples the wire to ledger retention (`docs/jamf-observations.md:309` reserves the right to compact). Trade: the values are the ledger's canonical form, not Jamf's raw bytes — NFC-normalised and stripped strings (`contract.py:75-76`), every spelling of absence dropped (`:114-140`; one app in the real fixture, `BambuStudio.app`, reports `"cfBundleVersion": null`, which becomes an absent key), byte-identical entries collapsed (`:525-526`), digest order rather than Jamf's order (`:532`). Against the 83 apps of `computer_inventory_detail_real.json` none of that changes a single string value; it can, in principle. The reading of "as is" this rests on is *names and field set*, which is the reading #81's ruling comment records.

**(b) Four new columns** on `installed_apps`, written at `service.py:968-981`. Trade: a migration, ~100 rows × four columns per device for data nothing but the wire reads, and a third copy of bytes `observation_entries` already stores once per tenant (`schema.py:957-972`). Decisive against it: columns solve the app section only. The other thirteen wrappers have no rows to read — `Device` holds a dozen scalars (`schema.py:128-153`) and there is no certificates or profiles table — so (b) needs (a) for everything else anyway.

**Recommend (a).** The snapshot is one object, read from one place, and it agrees with the ledger byte for byte — which is what makes a `device.inventory` sub-event and a `device.change` derived from the same span (#223) join on equal strings. If the session judges "as is" to mean Jamf's bytes, the variant is (a′): apply the same allowlist to `raw` with the contract's own selector (`_select`, `contract.py:153-174`) and skip `_prune`; same field set, raw values, empty strings kept — at the cost of re-implementing the EA merge and quarantine (`:543-563`) for the wire, which is the two-copies failure #197 exists to end.

Under either, the join to the `InstalledApp` row for `patch{}` is on `version_hash` — and the two sides hash different strings unless the session makes them agree. The rows hashed Jamf's **raw** strings: `normalize_computer` passes `name`, `bundleId`-or-`name` and `version` untouched with `short_version=None` (`client.py:734-741`) into `apply_hashes` (`service.py:126-139`), and `compute_version_hash` joins them on `:` with no normalisation (`backend/app/core/hashing.py:27-41`); the entry body is NFC-normalised and stripped (`contract.py:75-76`, `:122-124`). So hash exactly what the row hashed — the raw item strings with `short_version=None` (the `NormalizedApp` list `process_sync` already holds, hashed at `:890-891`, is that side), never the canonical body — or key both sides on the canonicalised `(name, bundleId-or-name, version)` tuple. A canonical-versus-raw mismatch is a silent `supported: false` on every affected app, and the fixture cannot catch it: all 83 names canonicalise to themselves. The pure test includes one name with trailing whitespace or a decomposed accent and asserts `supported: true`. A genuine miss is `supported: false` plus a log line, never an exception.

### `patch{}` and `vuln{}` on every app item

Both ride the snapshot because fatten-at-enqueue leaves the fan-out nothing to join against. In this session they are exactly:

- `patch`: `{"supported": <bool>}` — `true` iff the row's `jamf_title_ids` names at least one title (`None` is "no titles", `schema.py:220-221`; the session confirms the mapping against `summarize()` in `backend/app/mdm/patch/matching.py`). What the block holds when `true` is ruled — #68 closed 2026-09-02 (PR #239, `docs/jamf-patch-matching.md:152-162`): the clock is `first_newer_released_at`, unbounded; the sentence is a date plus `releases_missed`; raw values on the wire, buckets renderer-side. Populating those keys on the sub-event is a follow-on under clause 1; #113 owns `vuln{}`. Nothing beyond `supported` is minted here.
- `vuln`: `{"assessment": "off"}` — the discriminator populated from night one so presence is searchable (`vuln.assessment=off` extracts to a field; `{}` does not — the spike's Q3 argument, which survived the vocabulary change). `covered` and `unknown_app` arrive with #113's work.

### Aperture

The snapshot carries a section iff that section was in the read's aperture. `observation.sections` is built from `sections` and nothing else (`contract.py:590-598`), so this is free. A webhook collection scoped to `["general", "hardware", "operating_system"]` — the case `test_narrow_webhook_scope_never_wipes_apps` builds (`backend/tests/test_jamf_sync_e2e.py:277`) — produces a snapshot with three wrappers and no `app` key; a full read of a device with no apps produces `"app": []` (`:308`). This is the 2026-08-29 ruling applied per section: never assert an absence the read did not observe.

It generalises the spike's accepted carve-out on #81 — when `device.apps is None` "the snapshot event is **not** emitted" — to every section, and supersedes that wording: the event still fires; the unread section is what is absent. The other thirteen wrappers need the same rule, and a section-less snapshot cannot exist; #81's ruling comment carries this per-section reading. The two differ only on scoped webhook reads. If the session prefers the carve-out as written — emit nothing when `app` is outside the aperture — it says so in the PR and the doc, and gets clause 4 back for free. `webhook_scope` falls back to the whole contract when no webhook collection exists (`service.py:783-784`), so a snapshot always carries at least one section.

### `occurredAt`, envelope, `deviceMeta` — reused as-is

`occurredAt = event_time(device.last_inventory_at)` (`service.py:1020`; the rule at `backend/app/core/runs.py:160-187`, `docs/runs.md:69-79`): a sweep's snapshots share the run's window, a webhook's carries `reportDate`. The envelope is `envelope(occurred_at=…, host=existing.hostname, source=instance_label(connection.base_url))` (`:1032-1036`), lifted off at delivery by `_build_body` (`outbox.py:114-115`). `deviceMeta = _device_meta(existing)` (`:1021`), stamped **once**, on the snapshot's top level. Copying it onto every sub-event is #242's job, and the "over half the raw feed" cost (`payload.py:129-132`) is paid there, not here. No `deviceMeta` change is proposed: #189 owns the block, #220 owns the `jobID` path.

A snapshot and the delta from the same pull therefore share `occurredAt`, `jobID` and `eventID` — by design (#81 ruling 4: one id per device per pull, stamped on every event of that pull).

## `KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES` and the subscription default — decide, don't discover

`Destination.subscribed_events` null or empty means every event (`schema.py:738-741`, `outbox.py:293-294`, pinned at `test_outbox_passes_db.py:231`). Adding `device.inventory` to `KNOWN_EVENT_TYPES` (`outbox.py:21`) therefore means **every destination on the default subscription starts receiving one ~28 KB document per device per sweep** — generic webhooks and Elastic included — the day this merges. That is the spike's first named consequence, and it needs an answer rather than a default.

The `run.failed` precedent (`backend/migrations/versions/a9d4c7e1f3b8_run_failed_default_on.py`) went two ways at once: null stayed "all", *and* explicit lists had the new type appended, "so a failed run is loud everywhere unless an org deliberately unsubscribes". **Recommend the first half only:**

- Null/empty keeps meaning all. Carving one type out of the catch-all would give `null` a second meaning, which that migration's own docstring refused to do ("touching them would narrow their meaning").
- No append to explicit lists. A destination that curated its list never asked for a state stream; the reason `run.failed` was pushed — a failure must be loud — has no analogue for a 28 KB-per-device snapshot.
- Say in `docs/splunk-setup.md` what each destination type receives. A `splunk_hec` destination gets the snapshot wrapped in `{"event": …}` with `time`/`host`/`source` and no `sourcetype` (`outbox.py:117-138`) until #242. A generic webhook, and the `runreveal` preset, get the bare document (`:140-143`). An Elastic destination gets one `create` document per snapshot with `@timestamp` from `occurredAt` (`:154-178`), nested `app[]` and all — the multivalue-pairing hazard `docs/splunk-event-shaping.md:74-88` describes; per-app expansion for Elastic is not v0 (#81's blocker 2 is Splunk-scoped), and the doc should say so rather than let a customer find out.
- Opting out is `subscribed_events` on the API (`schemas/destinations.py:115`). The UI carries the field but has no editor for it — `frontend/src/features/destinations/types.ts:18-20` is the only mention of the field in `frontend/src`, beside one line of prose in `frontend/src/i18n/en.ts` — so say that too.

Before the flip the only destinations that exist are Kyle's, so the decision is cheap now and permanent later.

## Storage, retention and the worker — the consequences, measured where I could

**Size.** Built from `computer_inventory_detail_real.json` through the contract's own canonicalizer (`canonicalize_computer`, imported directly), under the full aperture, in the shape above, as compact JSON: **28,234 bytes** for one device with a synthetic thirteen-key `deviceMeta`. The fixture-derived halves are exact — 22,324 bytes of `app` list (83 items at ~269 bytes each, ~204 for Jamf's seven fields and ~65 for the two enrichment blocks) and 5,304 bytes for the other thirteen sections together; the ~430-byte head (`event`, `occurredAt`, `deviceMeta`) varies with the meta values. The same device's delta event on a baseline sweep is ~26.3 KB by the README's own arithmetic (509 + 311 × 83 = 26,322, `README.md:13`). So a snapshot costs roughly what a baseline costs today — **every sweep, not once**. It is the spike's 25–35 KB estimate, now measured on one real record.

**Outbox.** At the codebase's own design target of 40,000 devices (`outbox.py:30-31`, `:44-46`): ~1.1 GB of JSONB per sweep; a nightly sweep under the default `event_outbox_retention_days = 7` (`backend/app/core/config.py:45`, purged from `backend/app/main.py:215`) steady-states around 8 GB of rows in `event_outbox` before TOAST compression, which I did not measure.
